correctness.rationale: An unselected two-subset is undominated exactly when it is a two-vertex cover of the selected edge graph; a selected cover would be isolated in the induced Kneser graph, precluding a perfect matching. Four-edge component decompositions yield exactly four candidates of cover number >=3, and the triangle-plus-isolated-edge case has induced star K1,3 and is excluded. The three survivors have explicit pairings. Their support automorphism denominators 4,16,384 give the three binomial counts for every \(n\ge6\). For \(n=4\) the disjoint 3K2 structure is decisive. For \(n=5\) a complete 210-complement census separates six induced Petersen types and 125 matching/dominating complements in 3 S5-orbits. The exact standalone verifier independently checks all four-subsets through n=10, both predicates, all \(n=4,5\) minimum sizes, and \(n=5\) symmetry.

originality.rationale: Searched same-family and alias formulations in published research and published-finding corpus. The strongest full-text Kneser source (Cornet–Torres Lemma 18) characterizes ordinary k-tuple coverage without a matching requirement; its table gives ordinary minima, not paired four-edge types or the all-n polynomial. The 2014 extremal paired-domination paper varies the host graphs rather than classifying paired sets in \(\operatorname{KG}(n,2)\). published-finding corpus closest studies concern other graph families. value.rationale: A natural paired-monitoring optimization problem on the entire two-subset Kneser family receives a complete classification of all equality cases, not merely the minimum number. Three graph-structural support classes give a closed, parameter-uniform enumerator and precisely determine when each optimal symmetry type first appears. The exceptional Petersen graph yields an exact count and orbit refinement. This distinguishes backup-compatible domination from ordinary minimum domination, a gap motivated by the original paired-domination definition and ongoing Kneser domination literature. The statement is not an arbitrary local numerical slice or a recomputation of a known table.
